tweets.text:
There's still whitespace for vertical AI startups.

If you’re building vertical AI, look for four things in a market:

- The work repeats often enough to learn from
- Judgment matters, so there’s nuance to learn
- An expert can quickly evaluate the output and explain what to improve
- You can start with one task and grow into owning more of the job

Together, these can create a strong learning loop. That’s a key part of the vertical AI advantage. Focus can earn deeper access, more job-specific data and context, and a better understanding over time of what good work looks like.

Incumbents may own the record. Labs may own the front door. Vertical AI can still own the job.

a16z’s @seema_amble on where vertical AI can still win: https://t.co/iXt6sYNljU

BREAKING: ~54% of goods and services in the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) basket have recorded price increases of more than 3% over the last 12 months, near the highest proportion in 3 years.

This metric has surged +16 percentage points since Q1 2025.

By comparison, the 2022 peak was ~77%, while the 12-month average is ~37%.

However, this percentage remains significantly above the ~32% average seen in the 20 years before the 2020 pandemic.

To put this into perspective, during the 2012-2019 period, this figure never materially exceeded 30%.

The fight against inflation is far from over.

Affirm CEO Max Levchin on what it was like being around Elon Musk and the rest of the PayPal Mafia in the company's early days:

"We knew the people in the room intimately. We literally exchanged pheromones by hanging out in these sweaty rooms brainstorming, screaming at each other, spending a lot of time at whiteboards and declaring the other person's ideas idiotic."

"We knew the true version of that person. The ultra philosophical Peter Thiel, the go all in every time Elon Musk, the these days gubernatorial David Sacks."

"They all have the presentation layer, then what they're like at a dinner party, and then what they are when they're really stressed out and their head hurts and they don't know what to do."

"So as you watch one of these people go for something really big, like Elon taking humanity to Mars, which is extraordinary, you know he's a human being. I've seen him sweaty and tired and grumpy at the company kitchen a thousand times."

"They're not gods, they're humans. That inspires you to think, if that guy who's just a normal dude, I spent a lot of time with him, he's normal, and he's going for this big of an idea, I should strive too."

@mlevchin

Affirm CEO Max Levchin on why the card payment interface remains unbeaten, and why better ideas fail without reaching critical mass:

"We're forever in search of the great way to pay biometrically, and it manifests itself more in movies where people's thumbs and eyeballs get removed for authentication purposes."

"And yet we're still paying with chips. By the way, the card payment interface is the singular best user interface ever created."

"Even before PayPal there was this wand... where you could wave this wand next to a gas station and payment is secured and you can fuel your car. When I saw it I was like, this is obviously going to take over credit cards. And it didn't."

"Therein lies a really interesting lesson in payments innovation... There's not really an okay outcome in payments. You either get there and everyone needs to have your widget or your network, or it just goes into the annals of time."

"It made a lot of sense. Of course you want a little wand on your car keys, just wave and get refilled. But it's just a little bit faster, not a lot faster, than the credit card you have in your pocket that just works."

"I keep waiting for some completely different way of authenticating the payer to the device, and other than the mobile phone we haven't done better."

@mlevchin @eriktorenberg

The AI inside your business software no longer just offers to look things up for you. Salesforce updates the pipeline, Docusign redlines contacts, Workday runs HR and finance tasks.

Incumbents are upgrading from retrieval to agentic action.

a16z's Seema Amble says there's still room for startups to compete. No single record understands real work, because real work touches all systems a company runs on. Do the whole job better than anyone and you unlock a learning loop that compounds.

"The incumbent may own the record and the lab may control the front door, but the vertical AI company can still win by becoming the best at doing the job itself."

tweets.text: A bond left for dead just became one of the best trades of the year. Venezuela's defaulted 2027 note has climbed from about 20 cents on the dollar to 54 as the US built up forces in the Caribbean, removed Maduro, and struck a deal handing Washington control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. A restructuring that could top $200 billion is next. At 54 cents, the market still prices recovery at under a third of face value, a pure bet that Trump's deal holds and output ramps toward 1.5 million barrels a day. The bigger signal for everyone else: 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude are coming back under US control, and that is a long-term weight on oil prices.

Every other kind of private construction, homes, shops, offices, fell by $120 billion over the same stretch. One line item is holding up the entire construction economy, and it runs on hyperscaler capex that can be cut in a single earnings call. Broadcom just guided softer on AI chips. If the data-center spend slows, there is nothing underneath it, and the resilient economy story goes with it.

tweets.text: Europe is walking into winter with the gas tank near empty. EU storage is at a 15-year low, about 65% full, against a rule that says it must hit 90% by November 1. Europe delayed buying on a bet the Iran war would end fast. It did not, LNG just hit a 3.5-year high, and European buyers are now bidding against Asia for every cargo. This is a supply shock and a one-time price spike, the kind that fades once winter passes. It squeezes European industry that is already uncompetitive and hands pricing power to US LNG exporters selling into the panic. $LNG

thread_tweets.text:
It could be...CIFR facilities are very near the gas fields and pipeline can be incredibly cheap transmission compared to the generation they enable. Presumably someone else would operate the generators like SEI.

Which is where the questions start, since SEI-type deals are fixed-fee rental with the customer taking fuel risk. So the main one is what capital gets committed before a lease is signed, and who bears the fuel. It helps that CIFR is in the Permian, where gas is a byproduct and a producer takes that risk for almost free.
